title: Why Don't You - Yes But

source.quote: You sound like you have a problem. What do you want me to do about it?

setting: Thursday night support circle, five chairs. Farah just opened with: "I just wish my husband would learn to fix things around the house instead of always calling someone." Leena, Oskar, and Theo are already leaning in with ideas.

L1.line: Yes, but he'd see right through that, he'd know it was a hint.
cues: third suggestion rejected in a row
she leans forward for each new idea, like she's enjoying the hunt
never once says "I don't want advice"
L1.question: Three suggestions, three polite rejections, and Farah keeps leaning in for more. What's actually going on?

options.text: She genuinely wants a solution and just hasn't heard the right one yet.
options.feedback: If that were true, the room would drift toward specifics - budgets, schedules, actual logistics. Instead every idea gets a quick, generic "yes, but" and the group moves straight to the next one. That's not how real problem-solving sounds.

options.text: She's testing the group to see who cares enough to keep trying.
options.feedback: Close, but that reads intent into her rather than naming the structure of the exchange. What's actually observable is a repeating transaction shape, not a sincerity test.

options.text: The group is playing Why Don't You...? and Farah is playing Yes, But... - the point was never to find a workable suggestion.
options.feedback: Right. This is a game, not a problem-solving session: the social level says "help me," the psychological level says "you won't," and every exchange confirms it. The Response stage can run through ten suggestions as easily as three - the number was never the point.

options.text: Leena, Oskar, and Theo aren't actually listening to each other.
options.feedback: They're listening fine, and taking turns politely - the game doesn't need anyone to be rude or distracted, just willing to keep offering solutions.

L1.lesson: Why Don't You...? and Yes, But... are the same game from two chairs: the group supplies an endless Response stage of suggestions, and the presenter's Gimmick - a belief that she can't actually be helped, or doesn't want to be - rejects each one. The content of the suggestions is almost irrelevant, because the shape, not the specifics, is what's repeating.

L2.intro: Three suggestions down, three "yes, buts" collected. The room turns to you.

beats.line: I don't know... maybe nothing's going to work. You probably think I'm hopeless too.
cues: directly invites you, the leader, to either rescue or confirm hopelessness
group goes quiet, waiting on you

options.text: No, no, you're not hopeless, let me think... what about couples counseling?
options.outcome: Farah brightens for a second. "Yes, but we tried that two years ago and it didn't help." Round four begins.
options.lesson: Offering a fourth suggestion - even a warm, well-meant one - re-enters the Response stage exactly where everyone else has been standing. Reassurance plus a new idea is still fuel for Why Don't You...? Worth remembering for next time: the real skill here isn't getting it right once with Farah, it's doing the same antithesis again with the next person who starts a new round - like Leena, right after.

options.text: You're not hopeless, and I'm also not going to try to fix your husband from here.
options.outcome: Farah blinks, slightly thrown. "Oh. Okay." The group looks unsure what happens next.
options.lesson: This correctly declines to Rescue, and stops short of actually redirecting the conversation anywhere - it closes a door without opening the one that matters. And the harder part of this skill is still ahead: doing it again, on purpose, the next time someone else in the circle starts the same pattern - not just managing to say the right thing once.

options.text: That's a difficult problem. What are you going to do about it?
options.outcome: A real silence. Farah opens her mouth for a "yes, but" and finds there's nothing being offered to say yes-but to. "...I... hadn't thought about it that way."
options.lesson: This is the classic antithesis to Why Don't You...? / Yes, But...: it hands the problem back to the person who actually has it, in Adult, without supplying a target for the next rejection.

beats.line: Must be nice. My boss doesn't listen to ME either, and believe me, I've tried everything.
cues: same shape as Farah's opening, new content
group already leaning in with fresh ideas

options.text: Well, have you tried talking to HR about it?
options.outcome: "Yes, but HR is friends with my boss," Leena says instantly. The whole group is off again.
options.lesson: A fresh "why don't you" from you, the facilitator, re-opens exactly the game you just closed with Farah - the lesson doesn't transfer by accident, it has to be applied again, on purpose, to the new presenter.

options.text: Sounds like you want some advice too - go ahead, maybe someone has an idea.
options.outcome: The group dives in with five new suggestions. Leena fields each one with a "yes, but" of her own.
options.lesson: Handing the floor to the group restarts their Response stage - you've stepped out of Rescuer only to immediately wave everyone else back into it.

options.text: That's a hard one too. What have you actually decided to do about it?
options.outcome: Leena pauses, same as Farah did. "Huh. I don't think I've actually decided anything yet."
options.lesson: Applying the same antithesis to a new presenter, on purpose, is the actual skill - not a trick that works once on Farah, but a move for the pattern itself, wherever it shows up next.

options.text: Interesting how that came up right after Farah's did.
options.outcome: Leena shrugs. "I mean... I guess. Still true though." The observation lands but doesn't actually close anything.
options.lesson: Noticing the pattern out loud is useful and incomplete - naming it isn't the same as handing the problem back to the person who has it.

fields.label: Write the full Formula G for Farah's game: her Con, the group's Gimmick, what happened during the Response, the Switch, the Crossup, and the Payoff for both sides.
In under 50 words: why is "That's a difficult problem, what are you going to do about it?" an antithesis and not just a clever comeback?
Name one of the six advantages Farah gets from playing Yes, But... instead of actually fixing the problem.

echo.setting: Next week's circle. A sixth chair is empty, but a new member opens with the exact same shape Farah used.
echo.line: I just wish somebody around here would actually listen to me for once.
